draft.title: Samples and bias
card: A census collects data from every member of the population. It is accurate but often costly and slow.
A sample collects data from only some of the population. It is quicker and cheaper, but its results are only an estimate of the whole population.
A sample is biased if it favours some members of the population over others. A sample of volunteers or friends may be biased, because those people may differ from everyone else.
A random sample gives every member an equal chance of being chosen, which reduces bias. A larger sample usually gives a more reliable estimate.
draft.remember: A good sample is chosen at random and is large enough, so it can stand in for the population.

a.q: Which sampling method is most likely to reduce bias?
opts: Choosing students by drawing names from a full class list
Asking the students who sit near the front of the class
Asking only the students who offer to answer the survey
Asking the friends of the person who writes the survey
a.why: Drawing names from a full list gives every student an equal chance of being chosen. The other methods favour some students, such as those who volunteer, so they may not represent the group.
a.clue: Which method gives everyone an equal chance?

b.q: Priya wants to know how Year 10 students at her school travel to school. She asks 15 members of her own netball team. Why might her results be unreliable?
opts: Her sample is not random, so it may not represent Year 10
Her sample is a census, so the results are too costly
Her sample is random, so it has too few students
Her sample is too large, so it cannot be checked
b.why: Netball team members are not chosen at random, and they may travel differently from other students. This can make the sample biased. It is not a census, because it does not ask everyone.
b.clue: Would a netball team look like all of Year 10?

a.best: Choosing students by drawing names from a full class list

b.best: Her sample is not random, so it may not represent Year 10
